item.dc:creator: ロイター
item.content:encoded:
欧州市場サマリー（8日） 3:52 配信

＜ロンドン株式市場＞

続落して取引を終えた。中型株で構成するＦＴＳＥ２５０種指数は０．３９％安だった。原油価格急騰によるインフレ懸念と長期金利の上昇が相場の重荷となった。

英１０年債利回りは一時５．５２７％と１９年ぶりの高水準を付けた。２０年債、３０年債の利回りはいずれも６％を超えた。

ＦＴＳＥ３５０種石油・ガス株指数は３．７４％高。石油大手のＢＰは４．１％、シェルは３．６％それぞれ上昇した。

一方、銀行株指数は１．８０％安。金融大手ＨＳＢＣは１．９％、スタンダード・チャータードは２．０％、ロイズは１．７％、それぞれ値下がりした。

製薬・バイオテクノロジー株指数は２．２４％安。

スーパーマーケット大手のテスコは５．２％高。通期利益見通しを上方修正し、買われた。

ロンドン株式市場：[.LJP]

＜欧州株式市場＞

続落して取引を終えた。ＳＴＯＸＸ欧州６００種指数は約４カ月ぶりの安値を付けた。原油高によるインフレ懸念や長期金利上昇が相場の重荷となり、銀行株など大半の業種の株価が下落した。財政懸念が強いフランスのＣＡＣ４０指数は０．５１％安と、約半年ぶりの安値を付けた。

ＳＴＯＸＸ欧州６００種銀行株指数は２．０４％安。ドイツ銀行は０．７％、フランスのソシエテ・ジェネラルは２．３％、スペインのサンタンデールは２．９％、イタリアのウニクレディトは３．１％、いずれも下落した。

ヘルスケア株指数は２．４７％安。欧州のバイオ医薬品会社アルジェニクスは１５．９％下落した。シェーグレン病の臨床試験で主要目標を達成する見込みが薄いとして試験を中止したことを受け、売られた。

原油先物価格の値上がりを受けて、石油・ガス株指数は２．４２％上昇した。

欧州株式市場：[.FJ]

＜ユーロ圏債券＞

原油価格の急騰を受けてインフレ懸念が強まる中、域内国債利回りが上昇した。ただ、フランスやイタリアなど債務残高が大きい国の国債売りをいったん手控える動きが見られた。

８日の北海ブレント先物は一時、５％高の１バレル＝１０５ドルと、１週間ぶりの高値を付けた。米・イラン戦争や、イエメンの親イラン武装組織フーシ派とサウジアラビアとの紛争を背景に、中東からの原油供給途絶が懸念されている。

エネルギー価格の上昇を受け、市場では欧州中央銀行（ＥＣＢ）による追加利上げ観測が強まった。

ユーロ圏の指標となるドイツ１０年債利回りは２ベーシスポイント（ｂｐ）上昇の３．５０％。

ＥＣＢの政策金利見通しに敏感な独２年債利回りは５ｂｐ上昇の３．０８％。

フランス１０年債利回りは２ｂｐ上昇の４．８８％。取引序盤には９ｂｐ上昇する場面もあった。

独仏１０年債利回り格差は１３８ｂｐと２ｂｐ拡大した。

イタリア１０年債利回りは１ｂｐ低下の４．６３％となった。

ユーロ圏金融・債券市場：[DE/BJ]

item.title: ＦＲＢ、物価目標達成に追加利上げ必要＝セントルイス連銀総裁
item.description:
Michael S. Derby
[ニューヨーク ８日 ロイター] - 米セントルイス地区連銀のムサレム総裁は８日、連...
item.dc:creator: ロイター
item.content:encoded:
ＦＲＢ、物価目標達成に追加利上げ必要＝セントルイス連銀総裁 3:31 配信

２０２５年２月撮影　REUTERS/Brendan McDermid

Michael S. Derby

[ニューヨーク　８日　ロイター] - 米セントルイス地区連銀のムサレム総裁は８日、連邦準備理事会（ＦＲＢ）はインフレ率を目標の２％に戻すために追加利上げを実施する必要があると述べた。ただ、今月下旬の連邦公開市場委員会（ＦＯＭＣ）での対応については言及を避けた。

ムサレム氏はニューヨークで開かれたブルームバーグ主催のイベントで「インフレ率を適時に目標へ戻すには一段の金融引き締めが必要になる」とし、「『適時』を１８カ月程度と考える場合、向こう６─９カ月の適切な時期に追加利上げが必要になることを示唆している」と語った。

ＦＲＢは２７─２８日のＦＯＭＣで利上げを決定すべきかとの質問に対しては「毎回の会合に極めてオープンな姿勢で臨んでおり、その会合の結果や自分がどう行動するかについて予断を持っていない」と述べるにとどめた。ただ、「インフレ動向を踏まえると、追加的な政策引き締めを検討する必要がある」と述べた。ムサレム氏は今年のＦＯＭＣで投票権を持っていない。

このほか、力強い経済成長と安定した労働市場が続く中で、インフレが米経済にとって最大の課題になっていると指摘。雇用を大きく損なうことなくインフレ率を引き下げられる可能性が高く、ＦＲＢが目標とする２％に戻すことで経済全体に幅広く恩恵をもたらすことができるとの見方を示した。

このところ上昇している国債利回りについては、ＦＲＢに対する信認が失われていることを示すものではなく、経済が堅調で資本需要が強い環境下では実質金利が上昇するとの見方が背景にあると指摘。ハイテク部門の旺盛な投資や政府の巨額な資金調達需要も利回りを押し上げる要因になっていると述べた。同時に「米政府は過去２０年近くにわたり持続不可能な財政運営の軌道をたどっている」とし、多額の政府債務が経済に問題を引き起こすリスクが存在すると警告した。

FAST

WASHINGTON, Oct 8 : The four leaders of US President Donald Trump's AI task force are slated to meet on Thursday, task force vice chair Scott Kupor told Reuters, adding that he expects the full committee to convene next week as pressure builds on Washington to take action on AI. The task force is expected to help shape the administration's approach to AI at a pivotal moment for the technology.  Public uneasiness with AI, and the small group of people who seemingly hold sway over it, has risen in recent months. Most US voters think Trump's administration and Congress are not taking the risks of AI seriously enough and want the government to write new regulations for the technology, according to a Reuters/Ipsos poll published on Wednesday.  The AI companies "need to step up and demonstrate that they are taking concerns that people have around security and vulnerabilities very seriously, as do we," Kupor said.

Kupor said he expects the group to release a charter outlining its goals and responsibilities after its first full committee meeting. The group will have four to five staff members who will be assigned to the committee full-time, he said. Trump has dubbed the group the Super Intelligence Task Force, using his preferred term for artificial intelligence. It is led by Intelligence Director Jay Clayton, with Kupor, Federal Trade Commission Chair Andrew Ferguson and Defense Department technology lead Emil Michael. Trump calls the Defense Department the Department of War. Kupor said he will focus on engaging industries outside the technology sector, including banking, healthcare and utilities, to better understand how AI could affect their exposure to cyber threats. Michael will work directly with AI developers, Kupor said.

item.title: Trump says US will not attack Iran before midterm elections in November
item.description: President Donald Trump said on Thursday that the US will not launch an attack on Iran before November's US midterm congressional elections, asserting that the two countries are having "productive" talks about ending the six-month-old war.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: President Donald Trump said on Thursday that the US will not launch an attack on Iran before November's US midterm congressional elections , asserting that the two countries are having "productive" talks about ending the six-month-old war. "We are having productive discussions with the Islamic Republic of Iran," Trump wrote in a post on Truth Social. "We will not be attacking Iran at any time prior to the midterm elections to be held in the United States on November 3rd." The war, which began in February when the US and Israel launched strikes on Iran, has helped drive Trump's domestic approval ratings downward and is weighing heavily on his fellow Republicans as they seek to preserve their narrow legislative majorities in November's election. Some 60% of Americans — including one in four Republicans — disapprove of how Trump is handling the situation in Iran, according to a recent Reuters/Ipsos poll. The conflict has pushed gasoline prices sharply higher at a time when voters say their top concern is the cost of living. Trump has repeatedly said he expects oil prices to drop after the elections, but he has not offered a detailed plan for exiting the war. Iran and the US have exchanged proposals in recent weeks aimed at ending the war and reopening the Strait of Hormuz, a vital global energy shipping route. Trump rejected Tehran's latest offer. Iran's state media reported on Thursday that Tehran would not abandon uranium enrichment or hand over its uranium stockpile, citing the head of the country's Atomic Energy Organization, days after US Vice President JD Vance told Reuters that Iran must make "[USN:L1N45T0DK TEXT:"meaningful" reductions"] in its enrichment capacity. The US, Israel and Western allies have long accused Iran of seeking nuclear weapons, an accusation Iran has denied.

item.title: Shell partially restarts Pearl gas-to-liquids plant in Qatar
item.description: Shell said on Thursday it had partially restarted its Pearl gas-to-liquids plant in Qatar, as traders said QatarEnergy returned Pearl-GTL naphtha cargoes to the spot market six months after the facility was damaged during the Iran war.
item.dc:creator: Mohi Narayan, Stephanie Kelly, Shadia Nasralla
item.content:encoded: Shell (SHEL.L) said on Thursday it had partially restarted its Pearl gas-to-liquids plant in Qatar, as traders said QatarEnergy returned Pearl-GTL naphtha cargoes to the spot market six months after the facility was damaged during the Iran war. Shell said the move would allow it to build a limited amount of product inventory in storage, while its ability to ship product remains subject to the regional security situation. QatarEnergy has begun offering cargoes that include Pearl-GTL naphtha and resumed some contractual deliveries, signalling some return of products from the facility to a supply-starved market. The war disrupted refinery operations and temporarily shut the Strait of Hormuz, through which about 20% of global oil and liquefied natural gas supplies previously passed. Several traders who participate in the market said QatarEnergy issued a spot tender offering up to 50,000 metric tons of naphtha f four grades including Pearl GTL on a free-on-board basis from Ras Laffan port inside the Strait of Hormuz. The state-owned refiner's last naphtha tender, which also included Pearl GTL grade, was awarded at a discount of $150 to Middle East quotes on FOB basis. It [USN:L4N45R0QO TEXT:"has resumed"] sending contract volumes of naphtha to some buyers. India's Haldia Petrochemicals received its 50,000 metric tons for this quarter, a company executive said on Monday. Shell did not comment on the market tender and QatarEnergy did not respond to a request for comment. Oil companies typically do not comment on tenders. REPAIRS TO TRAIN 2 EXPECTED IN Q1 2027 Shell's wholly owned Pearl, which is fed from Qatar's North gas field, was [USN:L6N4070VH TEXT:"hit"] in March, damaging one of its two processing plants, also known as trains. At full capacity, Pearl can produce 140,000 barrels of oil equivalent per day. Pearl's output also feeds into Shell's downstream supply chain, including its lubricants business. Repairs to the facility's Train 2 are expected to be completed in the first quarter of next year, a Shell spokesperson said. Shell estimated in March that it would take one year to fully repair Pearl. Shell said its ability to sustain safe and reliable operations at Pearl depends on regional security, including the safe passage of shipments through the Strait of Hormuz. The first LNG train under QatarEnergy's North Field East expansion project [USN:L1N45T0GE TEXT:"will be ready"] to start operation in November, two people aware of its plans said, offering Qatar a path to restoring some lost output.

item.title: Trump administration freezes green cards for Microsoft, IT firms, probes universities
item.description: The US suspended Microsoft , major IT outsourcers and software maker Adobe from a key green-card program on Thursday while opening probes into nine top universities, widening a crackdown it says targets fraud and protects American jobs.
item.dc:creator: Akash Sriram, Steve Holland
item.content:encoded: The US suspended Microsoft (MSFT.O) , major IT outsourcers and software maker Adobe (ADBE.O) from a key green-card program on Thursday while opening probes into nine top universities, widening a crackdown it says targets fraud and protects American jobs. Since taking office, US President Donald Trump has pursued a broad effort to reduce the number of foreign-born people in the US and curtail their pathway to residence and citizenship. Thursday's twin actions mark the broadest strike yet against skilled-worker immigration programs — potentially cutting off a common path to permanent residency for foreign tech workers — while putting some of the country's top research universities on notice. "There has been no company in the United States, unfortunately, that has abused the system more than Microsoft," Vice President JD Vance said. He said the company laid off 6,000 American workers last year while benefiting from 6,300 H-1B temporary worker visas and nearly 3,000 green cards. His comments came hours before Trump honored tech billionaires for their contributions to America, including Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella. Nadella once held an H-1B visa, as did Elon Musk, who was also honored, while three of the other CEOs honored are immigrants. Nadella thanked Trump for the medal, saying in a post on X he would continue to advance technology and drive American prosperity. Microsoft is the largest filer of PERM applications, or the [USN:L4N45U1DA TEXT:"permanent labor certification"] process, according to data from the US labor department. Under PERM, which most employment-based green cards require, employers must show a foreign hire will not hurt US workers' wages or jobs. The company said in a statement that about 80% of the H-1B applications it filed in the last fiscal year were to extend or change the status of current employees, not to hire new workers. In July, the company said it would [USN:L4N4380XC TEXT:"cut 4,800 jobs"], or about 2.1% of its global workforce. CRACKDOWN WIDENS Labor Secretary Keith Sonderling said the suspension would also cover Cognizant (CTSH.O) , Infosys (INFY.NS) , Tata Consultancy Services (TCS.NS) , Wipro (WIPR.NS) , HCL Technologies (HCLT.NS) and Capgemini (CAPP.PA) . "We will not accept any new or process any pending permanent labor certification applications involving these companies," Sonderling said. He said these companies had since 2009 sought almost three million foreign workers, and had received over 230,000 H-1B visa approvals and over 100,000 permanent labor certifications. Amazon.com was the largest employer of approved H-1B beneficiaries in fiscal 2026, followed by Tata Consultancy Services, Infosys, Apple and Microsoft, according to US immigration data. Vance said the suspensions would last "as long as it needs to," and that the administration wanted the companies to change how they hire. He said some companies post ineffective job ads, then point to the lack of applicants to justify hiring lower-paid foreign workers. Microsoft said in its statement that it pays its H-1B employees the same as any other employees doing comparable work. Adobe, Cognizant, Infosys, HCL Technologies, Wipro and Capgemini did not immediately respond to requests for comment. Tata Consultancy Services declined to comment. Nasscom, India's IT industry body, said Indian tech companies in the US had significantly reduced their reliance on H-1B visas, and relatively few of their workers sought green cards through the PERM process. In September last year, the Labor Department launched an enforcement drive called "Project Firewall" as a White House proclamation imposed a one-time $100,000 fee on new H-1B petitions for workers hired from abroad. UNIVERSITIES UNDER SCRUTINY Vance also said nine universities, including Harvard, Yale and Stanford, would be investigated for what the administration called the misuse of exchange-visitor visas to undercut American wages. The nine schools also include Brown and the Massachusetts Institute of Technology. Labor Inspector General Anthony D'Esposito said subpoenas had already been served. D'Esposito said investigators would examine whether foreign influence, improper financial relationships or visa abuse were compromising federally funded research. “It could have an enormous economic impact on the whole US economy,” said Sarah Spreitzer, a vice president at the American Council on Education, which represents college and university presidents. International students historically spent $40 billion a year while in the US, she said. The probe deepens the administration's [USN:L1N45M14M TEXT:"long-running fight"] with Harvard over foreign students. Last year, the Department of Homeland Security subpoenaed the university over alleged misconduct by international students and its compliance with immigration law. Harvard called that subpoena "unfounded retribution" but said it would comply as far as the law requires. Rapidly changing visa policies caused a sharp drop in international applications to Columbia University and contributed to the university pausing admissions to one of its journalism programs, Reuters reported last week.

item.title: Plane damaged at Riyadh airport as Houthis escalate attacks, sources say
item.description: Yemen's Iran-aligned Houthis escalated their campaign of strikes against Saudi Arabia on Thursday, trying to shut down the kingdom's airspace and oil facilities with missile fire that has killed three people this week and left a plane badly damaged.
item.dc:creator: Timour Azhari, Federico Maccioni
item.content:encoded: Yemen's Iran-aligned Houthis escalated their campaign of strikes against Saudi Arabia on Thursday, trying to shut down the kingdom's airspace and oil facilities with missile fire that has killed three people this week and left a plane badly damaged. The group said it had struck Riyadh airport and warned workers to stay away from energy plants, which would be targeted. Shrapnel from an interception or another projectile hit had left the commercial plane belonging to Saudi state carrier Saudia Airlines heavily damaged after catching fire while parked at an airport terminal on Thursday, three people briefed on the matter said. They said no passengers were believed to have been on the plane at the time but they could not rule out any injuries as a result of the incident. A thick black column of smoke and flames were shown rising from Riyadh airport in video verified by Reuters. Saudi Arabia's government media office, its civil aviation authority and Saudia Airlines did not respond to emailed requests for comment. Lufthansa and Air India said they were [USN:L6N45U10R TEXT:"suspending "]flights to Riyadh after Houthi attacks. Separately, Saudi officials said debris from an intercepted missile had hit a kindergarten and medical complex in Riyadh. The Houthis say they are targeting the kingdom over its support for government forces in Yemen's reignited civil war. Saudi Arabia says it is backing an offensive by Yemen's UN-recognised government to take back territory from the Houthis. The conflict, now an overspill of the US-Iran war , has added new chaos to a region already aflame, and threatens to draw other states into gruelling mountain fighting, with Syria now considering [USN:L1N45U05X TEXT:"deploying troops"] to assist Saudi Arabia. The kingdom has pushed for support from allied nations, including [USN:L6N45T0IX TEXT:"Turkey"] and Pakistan, even if only in a logistical or defensive capacity, as it tries to reverse Houthi gains in southwest Yemen, by the southern entrance to the Red Sea. Those requests have taken on more urgency since Saudi authorities said on Wednesday that three people had been [USN:L1N45T00S TEXT:"killed"] this week in strikes on Riyadh airport and Abha airport in the southwest. DELAYS AND CANCELLATIONS The Houthis have made Saudi airports a focus of their strikes, and the Saudi-led coalition fighting in Yemen said it had destroyed two ballistic missiles launched by the group towards Riyadh and another towards Khamis Mushayt, home to a major airbase. According to data compiled by aviation analytics company Cirium, almost half of departures from Riyadh airport had been cancelled by 1500 GMT, with 31 more cancellations expected for Friday in all Saudi airports. Flight tracker FlightRadar24 indicated numerous delayed arrivals and departures at Riyadh's King Khalid International Airport on Thursday. The airport advised travellers to contact airlines to check the status of flights before trying to travel. Riyadh is due to host a major meeting of energy policy makers, the WPC Energy Congress, this week. Several multinational firms based in Riyadh's King Abdullah Financial District (KAFD) told staff to work from home after loud booms were heard on Thursday morning, five people familiar with the matter said, including some affected staff. The Saudi government did not respond to a request for comment, and KAFD was not immediately available for comment. Some diplomats said they had received warnings, and some schools in Riyadh told parents there were orders to shelter in place, though authorities did not issue a public alert. Reuters could not identify the source of the booms. CIVIL WAR REIGNITED BY CONFLICT IN IRAN Yemen's long-running civil war, which paused with a ceasefire in 2022, has erupted again in recent weeks with the Houthis seizing stretches of the Red Sea coast last month, including along the vital Bab el-Mandeb Strait. Their threats to shipping and attacks on Saudi cities and infrastructure have drawn the kingdom back in. This week, Saudi-backed forces launched a [USN:L8N45M1W0 TEXT:"counterattack"], taking back some areas around the strait. However, in a war with several front lines, the Houthis have made gains of their own, surrounding Yemen's third-largest city, Taiz, by taking territory along its main mountain road to Aden. The fighting, which pits the Houthis against a coalition of [USN:L6N45S0PX TEXT:"Saudi-backed forces"] under the internationally recognised government, has led to a humanitarian crisis in the poorest Arab state, displacing 200,000 people since the conflict resumed. One US and one Syrian defence official said Syria was carefully considering options for military support, including defensive aid to protect Saudi Arabia from attacks, or an offensive deployment to help take the fight to the Houthis. In response to a request for comment to the Syrian foreign ministry, a diplomat said Syria stood firmly with Saudi Arabia but that its focus was on domestic priorities such as recovery from its own civil war. NATO-member Turkey said on Wednesday it was sending mainly defensive and technical support to the kingdom to help in the fight against the Houthis. A Turkish official said this was expected to take the form of military equipment, intelligence sharing and weapons systems.

item.title: French students keep up protest pressure with some demonstrations hit by violence
item.description: French teenagers blockaded some high schools and marched through cities on Thursday in the latest wave of nationwide protests about conditions in the country's schools, and some of the demonstrations were marred by violent unrest.
item.dc:creator: Manon Cruz, Dominique Vidalon
item.content:encoded: French teenagers blockaded some high schools and marched through cities on Thursday in the latest wave of nationwide protests about conditions in the country's schools, and some of the demonstrations were marred by violent unrest. The Interior Ministry said 71,500 people participated in the day's demonstrations, of which 24,500 took part in the main Paris protest centred around the Bastille square. The Paris protest was mostly peaceful, although there were occasional clashes between small groups of demonstrators and the police during the evening. Elsewhere, arsonists attacked a [USN:FWN45U1T1 TEXT:"Bordeaux"] police station, a school in Saint-Etienne was ransacked and a teacher in Toulouse was hit by a demonstrator, said the Interior Ministry. In Marseille, police said a teacher at Victor Hugo High School [USN:FWN45U1T4 TEXT:"was attacked"] during the latest protests and has filed a criminal complaint over the incident. Protesters clash with French gendarmes, as French high school and university students attend a demonstration, as part of a nationwide day of protests and blockades to demand better school conditions, in Nantes, France, October 8, 2026. REUTERS/Stephane Mahe A water cannon sprays protesters during a demonstration by French high school and university students in Paris as part of a nationwide day of protests and blockades supported by teachers and school parents to demand better school conditions in France, October 8. REUTERS/Abdul Saboor A protester kicks away a tear gas cannister during a demonstration by French high school and university students in Paris as part of a nationwide day of protests and blockades supported by teachers and school parents to demand better school conditions in France, October 8. REUTERS/Abdul Saboor Police officers clash with protesters during a demonstration by French high school and university students in Paris as part of a nationwide day of protests and blockades supported by teachers and school parents to demand better school conditions in France, October 8. REUTERS/Abdul Saboor Police use "flash-balls", as French high school and university students attend a demonstration, as part of a nationwide day of protests and blockades to demand better school conditions, in Nantes, France, October 8. REUTERS/Stephane Mahe A demonstrator is treated with milk after exposure to tear gas during nationwide protests in Paris, France, October 8, to demand better school conditions. REUTERS/Pedro Nunes Protestors, including French high school and university students attend a demonstration in Nantes, part of a nationwide day of protests and blockades to demand better school conditions in France, October 8. REUTERS/Stephane Mahe A protester confronts riot police officers outside Lycee Helene-Boucher high school as students block the road, during nationwide protests in Paris, France, on October 8, to demand better school conditions. REUTERS/Pedro Nunes A protester balances a barricade on his head as French high school and university students attend a demonstration in Nantes as part of a nationwide day of protests and blockades to demand better school conditions in France, October 8. REUTERS/Stephane Mahe A person kicks a tear gas canister as French high school and university students attend a demonstration, part of a nationwide day of protests and blockades to demand better school conditions, in Nantes, France, October 8. REUTERS/Stephane Mahe Police officers in riot gear clash with demonstrators during nationwide protests in Paris, France, October 8, to demand better school conditions. REUTERS/Pedro Nunes People attend a demonstration at Place de la Bastille, during nationwide protests to demand better school conditions, in Paris, France, October 8. REUTERS/Pedro Nunes A police officer in riot gear uses a truncheon during nationwide protests in Paris, France, October 8, to demand better school conditions. REUTERS/Pedro Nunes Demonstrators gather on the July Column in Place de la Bastille during nationwide protests to demand better school conditions in Paris, France, October 8, . REUTERS/Pedro Nunes Protesters gather at Place de la Bastille during a demonstration by French high school and university students, as part of a nationwide day of protests and blockades supported by teachers and school parents to demand better school conditions, in Paris, France, October 8. REUTERS/Abdul Saboor French students gather outside the Lycee Henri-IV in Paris as part of nationwide protests to demand better school conditions in France, October 8. REUTERS/Abdul Saboor French high school students sit on barricades outside the Lycee Lamartine high school in Paris, as part of nationwide protests to demand better school conditions in France, October 8. REUTERS/Pedro Nunes Protesters march during a demonstration by French high school students, as part of a nationwide day of protests and blockades, expressing anger over overcrowded classrooms, teacher shortages and dilapidated school buildings, which students blame on years of underinvestment, in Marseille, France, October 8. REUTERS/Manon Cruz A French high school student confronts people who want to prevent her from building a barricade, outside the Lycee Lamartine high school in Paris, as part of nationwide protests to demand better school conditions in France, October 8. REUTERS/Pedro Nunes Protesters face French CRS riot police outside Lycee Helene-Boucher high school as students block the road, during nationwide protests in Paris, France, October 8, to demand better school conditions. REUTERS/Pedro Nunes A person carries the French national flag as French high school and university students attend a demonstration, as part of a nationwide day of protests and blockades to demand better school conditions, in Nantes, France, October 8. REUTERS/Stephane Mahe People march during a demonstration by French high school students, as part of a nationwide day of protests and blockades, expressing anger over overcrowded classrooms, teacher shortages and dilapidated school buildings, which students blame on years of underinvestment, in Marseille, France, October 8. A banner reads: "Funding cut, youth sacrificed." REUTERS/Manon Cruz The protest movement, now into its third week, has exposed deep tensions in France between popular demands for investments in deteriorating public services and a cash-strapped government under [USN:L8N45S1P0 TEXT:"pressure from bond markets"] to reduce its debt and deficit. Protesters say they are demonstrating to demand more teachers and better facilities, arguing school buildings are often dilapidated, with overcrowded classrooms that are often freezing in winter and boiling in summer. Critics say the movement has been infiltrated by violent far-left and anarchist elements. High-school teacher Diane Di Sciullo joined students in Marseille, saying all they were asking for was a decent education in decent conditions. She denounced overcrowding, saying this year she had 37 students in her class. "At the start of every lesson, I have to ask them to check the neighbouring classrooms for spare chairs and desks so they can actually study," she said. Di Sciullo, 28, was carrying a placard that read, "I'm a teacher and my students help me catch cockroaches in class." MINISTER PROMISES URGENT ACTION Education ministry figures showed the number of school blockades was gradually decreasing. Education Minister Edouard Geffray told TF1 TV that extra teachers would be drafted in to plug gaps in schools which do not have enough teachers, while heavy school timetables will also be reviewed. It is not uncommon for French teenagers to have lessons from 8 a.m. to 6 p.m., as well as large amounts of homework. Geffray also said he was working on potential improvements to Parcoursup, the national online portal for applying to university, which has been widely criticised as confusing and stressful for applicants. Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu pledged late on Wednesday that the government would present "concrete, quick and fully funded responses" to the protests by late October, without offering specifics. Student protest leaders said that was not good enough and called for further marches next Tuesday. There are also calls circulating online for a day of protests on October 17. "Our demands must be heard. Yesterday, Mr Lecornu gave us a lot of hot air," said Ryad Rani, leader of one of the student unions. "The mobilisation will continue, we're not backing down on anything." A prominent complaint featured on banners and placards was that the police response to the wave of protests has been too heavy-handed. "Too young to be listened to, old enough to be tear-gassed" was one example. There have been hundreds of arrests and dozens of injuries since the movement started. On Wednesday, the government [USN:L1N45T0EM TEXT:"suspended the use of stun grenades"] in the policing of the protests after one [USN:L1N45R08Q TEXT:"teenager's hand was blown off"]. POLITICAL RESPONSE SHOWS POLARISATION AS ELECTION LOOMS Six months from a presidential election, the protests have highlighted stark polarisation between leading candidates to replace Emmanuel Macron, who cannot seek a third term. Far-right frontrunner Marine Le Pen has highlighted damage to schools caused by a minority of protesters and outlined [USN:L8N45R1J6 TEXT:"plans to slash public spending"] should she win. Her hard-left opponent Jean-Luc Melenchon, who also has a chance of making the runoff, has praised the protesters as "incredible" and denounced police brutality. According to an Elabe poll for BFM TV, 72% of French people think the students' demands are legitimate, but 55% of them think the protests should stop. Neighbouring [USN:L1N45T0NH TEXT:"Belgium"] has also had student protests, with demonstrations in Brussels, Ciney and Liege.

item.title: AirBaltic plans to cut up to 700 jobs (Oct. 5)
item.description: Latvian airline airBaltic said on Monday it is preparing to cut about 500 to 700 jobs across its bases in Riga, Vilnius and Tallinn.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: Latvian airline airBaltic said on Monday it is preparing to cut about 500 to 700 jobs across its bases in Riga, Vilnius and Tallinn. The carrier [USN:L6N4560BC TEXT:"filed"] for Chapter 11 bankruptcy in New York in September, aiming to complete a sweeping restructuring focused on cutting its mounting debt through capacity and fleet reductions AirBaltic gained [USN:L6N4580GU TEXT:"approval last month"] to access €140 million ($157 million) from a wider €350 million financing package. CEO Erno Hilden told Reuters in September that the airline [USN:L6N456122 TEXT:"was in talks"] with labour unions over "an adjustment" to the workforce New organisational structures for the rest of the company are expected to be defined by mid-October, airBaltic said, with the final number of layoffs potentially changing within the course of the process Dace Kavasa, chairperson of the Latvian aviation union, told Reuters the announcement could be seen as "pure union busting" as the airline did not disclose the potential number of layoffs with unions before making it public "We learned about 500 to 700 people, six minutes before they started an employee meeting where they presented this," Kavasa said, adding that any talks will only start on October 15 Unions have proposed staff to take 85% part-time work and are pushing towards offering 50%, Kavasa added ($1 = 0.8922 euros)

item.description: L'Europe vue dans le vert, accalmie sur le pétrole et les rendements
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: L'Europe vue dans le vert, accalmie sur le pétrole et les rendements 9 octobre (Reuters) - Les principales Bourses européennes sont attendues sur un rebond vendredi à l'ouverture, portées par la baisse des cours du pétrole et une accalmie sur le marché obligataire, même si la volatilité reste élevée en raison des craintes budgétaires dans des pays comme la France. La BCE pourrait devoir procéder à de nouvelles hausses de taux, estime Dolenc LJUBLJANA, 8 octobre (Reuters) - La Banque centrale européenne (BCE) pourrait être contrainte de continuer à relever ses taux directeurs face au risque d'une aggravation de l'inflation mais le moment et l'ampleur d'une telle mesure restent bien trop incertains pour pouvoir être prédits, a déclaré Primož Dolenc, membre du Conseil des gouverneurs de l'institution de Francfort et gouverneur de la banque centrale slovène. Le secteur du luxe freiné davantage par des mesures fiscales en Chine PARIS/PEKIN, 9 octobre (Reuters) - Le tour de vis enclenché par la Chine pour lutter contre l'évasion fiscale des plus fortunés est devenu un motif supplémentaire d'inquiétude pour les enseignes de luxe, lesquelles font déjà face aux répercussions de la guerre en Iran et à un ralentissement de la consommation aux Etats-Unis. Le gouvernement allemand relève ses prévisions de croissance pour 2026 et 2027 BERLIN, 8 octobre (Reuters) - Le gouvernement allemand a revu à la hausse ses prévisions économiques pour cette année et l'année prochaine, la guerre en Iran n'ayant pas un impact aussi sévère qu'initialement redouté, a déclaré jeudi le ministère de l'Economie. Zone euro: Les rendements obligataires se tendent encore LONDRES, 8 octobre (Reuters) - Les rendements obligataires de la zone euro enregistrent jeudi de nouvelles fortes tensions, dans un contexte de hausse des prix de l'énergie, les investisseurs continuant à se débarrasser des obligations des pays les plus endettés comme la France et l'Italie, provoquant un creusement des "spreads" dans le bloc. Aux yeux du patron de Ryanair, le coût du kérosène restera élevé une année de plus BRUXELLES/LONDRES, 8 octobre (Reuters) - Les compagnies aériennes européennes vont connaître une nouvelle année de coûts de carburant élevés et de taris en hausse, la guerre en Iran maintenant les prix du kérosène à un niveau supérieur d'environ 50% à celui d'avant le conflit, a déclaré jeudi Michael O'Leary, directeur général de Ryanair. Le choc géopolitique se répercute désormais sur les marchés financiers, selon Moulin (BCE) FRANCFORT, 8 octobre (Reuters) - La quasi-totalité du choc inflationniste subi par l'Europe cette année est liée à l'énergie, mais les chocs géopolitiques à l'origine de la flambée des prix "se traduisent désormais par un choc financier", a déclaré jeudi Emmanuel Moulin, gouverneur de la Banque de France (BdF) et membre de la Banque centrale européenne (BCE). BCE-Wunsch contre un relèvement du ratio de réserves obligatoires des banques FRANCFORT, 8 octobre (Reuters) - La projet de la Banque centrale européenne (BCE) visant à relever le ratio de réserves obligatoires imposé aux banques commerciales pourrait nuire à la crédibilité de ses futures opérations, voire empiéter sur la politique budgétaire des Etats, a déclaré jeudi Pierre Wunsch, membre du Conseil des gouverneurs de l'institution de Francfort et gouverneur de la Banque nationale de Belgique. Allemagne: Baisse surprise des exportations en août 8 octobre (Reuters) - Les exportations allemandes ont baissé de façon inattendue en août, accusant un recul de 0,8% par rapport au mois précédent, selon les données de l'Office fédéral de la statistique publiées jeudi. PepsiCo revoit à la baisse de ses prévisions, annonce de nouvelles réductions des coûts 8 octobre (Reuters) - PepsiCo a annoncé jeudi son intention de mettre en œuvre de nouvelles mesures de réduction des coûts après avoir revu à la baisse ses prévisions de bénéfice annuel récurrent, en raison d'une demande atone pour ses snacks et ses boissons en Amérique du Nord et de la hausse des coûts des matières premières.

item.title: OFRMO Summary
item.description: Trump dit qu'il s'abstiendra d'attaquer l'Iran avant les "midterms" aux USA
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: Trump dit qu'il s'abstiendra d'attaquer l'Iran avant les "midterms" aux USA WASHINGTON, 8 octobre (Reuters) - Le président américain Donald Trump a déclaré jeudi que les Etats-Unis ne lanceraient pas d'attaque contre l'Iran d'ici aux élections de mi-mandat au Congrès américain ("midterms") début novembre, ajoutant que Washington avait des discussions "productives" avec Téhéran. Les Etats-Unis et la Russie étudient la possibilité de vendre du gaz à l'Europe BERLIN/WASHINGTON, 8 octobre (Reuters) - De hauts responsables russes et américains ont discuté de la possibilité d'impliquer un investisseur américain dans les gazoducs Nord Stream qui alimentaient l'Allemagne en gaz russe avant l'invasion de l'Ukraine, ont dit à Reuters cinq personnes proches du dossier. El Niño a atteint son niveau le plus intense jamais enregistré - météo japonaise TOKYO, 9 octobre (Reuters) - Le phénomène El Niño a atteint en septembre son niveau le plus élevé jamais enregistré, a déclaré vendredi l'Agence météorologique japonaise, ajoutant qu'il y avait 100% de chances que ces conditions persistent pendant l'hiver de l'hémisphère nord. L'ouragan Isaias se renforce à l'approche des côtes américaines 8 octobre (Reuters) - L'ouragan Isaias s'est renforcé jeudi alors qu'il se dirigeait la côte des Etats-Unis dans le Golfe du Mexique, provoquant des évacuations et la déclaration de l'état d'urgence en Floride et dans l'Alabama alors que les météorologues ont mis en garde contre de dangereuses ondes de tempêtes, des tornades et des inondations. Schröder a célébré l'anniversaire de Poutine en Russie 8 octobre (Reuters) - L'ancien chancelier allemand Gerhard Schröder a participé à la célébration du 74e anniversaire du président russe Vladimir Poutine, a indiqué jeudi le Kremlin. Corée du Nord: Kim Yo Jong rejette l’aide médicale sud-coréenne, la qualifiant de provocation SÉOUL, 8 octobre (Reuters) - Kim Yo Jong, l'influente soeur du dirigeant nord-coréen Kim Jong Un, a dénoncé jeudi le projet de la Corée du Sud de fournir une aide sous forme de matériel médical à Pyongyang, qualifiant cette initiative de "provocation politique" et de violation de la souveraineté de son pays. Les Etats-Unis vont diffuser en direct l'exécution de l'auteur de la fusillade de Ford Hood WASHINGTON, 8 octobre (Reuters) - Les Etats-Unis vont diffuser en direct l'exécution de Nidal Hasan, qui avait tué 13 personnes sur la base militaire de Fort Hood au Texas en 2009, a déclaré un responsable du Pentagone. Ukraine: Une rue de Kramatorsk bombardée par la Russie, 33 morts KYIV, 8 octobre (Reuters) - Une frappe russe a fait au moins 33 morts et 18 blessés jeudi matin dans une rue de Kramatorsk, verrou stratégique des forces ukrainiennes dans le Donbass, ont rapporté les autorités locales. Le bilan de la vaste attaque russe en Ukraine mercredi passe à 32 morts Le bilan de la pluie de missiles et de drones russes qui s'est abattue sur l'Ukraine dans la nuit de mardi à mercredi est passé à 32 morts et 100 blessés après le décès de deux personnes tuées par des débris de drones mercredi soir dans une banlieue de Kyiv. Espagne: L'octogénaire symbole de la crise du logement est morte MADRID, 7 octobre (Reuters) - Maricarmen Abascal, Espagnole de 87 ans dont l'expulsion de son appartement madrilène le mois dernier a déclenché une vague de protestation contre la cherté de l'immobilier dans le pays, est décédée mercredi, a annoncé le syndicat des locataires de la capitale espagnole.

item.title: OFRTP Summary
item.description: Nobel/Littérature: Le prix décerné à la poète et écrivaine canadienne Anne Carson
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: Nobel/Littérature: Le prix décerné à la poète et écrivaine canadienne Anne Carson STOCKHOLM, 7 octobre (Reuters) - Le prix Nobel de littérature a été décerné jeudi à la poète et écrivaine canadienne Anne Carson pour "son oeuvre audacieuse et inventive qui, dans un dialogue ludique avec la tradition classique, a créé de nouvelles formes pour la littérature contemporaine", a annoncé jeudi l'Académie royale des sciences de Suède. L'Allemagne abandonne le projet de char commun avec la France-Mandon PARIS, 8 octobre (Reuters) - L'Allemagne a décidé d'abandonner le projet avec la France de char commun du futur, le MGCS ("Main Ground Combat System", système principal de combat terrestre), a annoncé jeudi le chef d'état-major des armées, Fabien Mandon, lors d'une audition devant une commission parlementaire. France-Dix millions de barils de gazole libérés des réserves pour baisser les prix à la pompe-Lecornu La France va libérer 10 millions de barils de gazole de ses réserves stratégiques avec l'objectif d'agir sur les prix à la pompe, qui devraient ainsi "mécaniquement baisser" de 12 centimes à 18 centimes d'euro par litre de gazole, a déclaré mercredi soir le Premier ministre Sébastien Lecornu. Le Danemark accuse la Russie d'actes de sabotage contre ses entreprises du secteur de la défense La Russie a lancé des opérations de sabotage contre des entreprises danoises fournissant l'Ukraine après avoir conclu que ses tentatives de perturbation à plus grande échelle n'avaient pas freiné le soutien militaire occidental à Kyiv, a déclaré mercredi une responsable des services de renseignement danois. Nuñez suspend l'usage des grenades assourdissantes contre les lycéens L'usage des grenades assourdissantes par les forces de l'ordre est suspendu "dans le cadre du mouvement lycéen", a annoncé mercredi sur RTL le ministre de l'Intérieur, Laurent Nuñez. De plus en plus d'enfants non accompagnés empruntent des voies dangereuses pour rejoindre l'Europe, selon l'Onu Plus des deux tiers des enfants réfugiés et migrants qui ont rejoint l'Europe par les routes de la Méditerranée et des Balkans en 2025 étaient non accompagnés et bon nombre d'entre eux ont été victimes d'exploitation, selon un rapport publié mercredi par des agences des Nations Unies. La France ne peut plus se permettre la moindre erreur sur ses finances publiques dit Citadel La France ne peut plus se permettre la moindre erreur dans l'assainissement de ses finances publiques et la pression exercée par les marchés devrait inciter le gouvernement à se concentrer sur la maîtrise des dépenses à l'approche de l'élection présidentielle de 2027, a déclaré à Reuters Angel Ubide, économiste chez la société de gestion d'actifs Citadel. Nobel/Chimie-Le Français Henri Kagan et le Japonais Kenso Soai distingués pour avoir résolu le mystère des molécules "images miroir" Le prix Nobel de chimie a été décerné mercredi à Henri Kagan et à Kenso Soai pour avoir résolu une énigme de longue date sur la manière de former une seule des deux "images miroir" d'une molécule, une découverte d'une grande importance pour la fabrication de médicaments, a annoncé mercredi l'Académie royale des sciences de Suède. États-Unis: Christa Pike est consciente et capable de parler selon ses avocats Christa Pike, dont l'exécution a échoué la semaine dernière dans le Tennessee, a repris conscience et retrouvé l'usage de la parole, ont déclaré ses avocats dans un communiqué publié mardi soir. Marine Le Pen veut ramener le déficit budgétaire à 3% d'ici 2030 La candidate du Rassemblement national pour l'élection présidentielle 2027 en France, Marine Le Pen, a déclaré mardi qu'elle souhaitait ramener le déficit budgétaire du pays à 3% d'ici 2030, invitant le pays à faire les "bons choix" sous peine de perdre son autonomie financière.
